title: Microprocessor to mass-market personal-computing platform
pressure: Custom logic and minicomputer-scale systems were costly to redesign; MOS integration opened programmable control, but a CPU chip alone did not create a personal-computing market.
preExistingWorldModel: Calculator-specific chip sets, minicomputers and embedded controllers were known; memory, I/O, software, displays and distribution remained separate constraints.
observationsAndInstruments: Intel converted a Busicom calculator request into the programmable 4004 family and later marketed the processor broadly.
Successive 8-bit CPUs plus EPROM/RAM/peripherals enabled complete microcomputers.
Altair/Apple-class systems exposed demand for software and peripherals.
IBM used off-the-shelf parts and published interfaces under a compressed schedule, enabling a compatible ecosystem.
decisiveTests: reuse one CPU architecture across materially different applications
technicalOrScientificTransition: Computing shifted from custom electronic logic to a programmable component platform and then to ecosystems in which software, interfaces and third-party complements often mattered more than the CPU alone.
rivalsAndFailures: The microprocessor began as a solution to a calculator contract, not a ready PC market.
Early kits remained niche until software/peripheral complements matured.
Open compatibility accelerated complements while reducing IBM control.
diffusionAndScaling: Diffusion depended on complements, cost/yield/standards and institutional adoption; the nominal breakthrough date did not equal broad effective use.
standardsAndInstitutions: Laboratories, firms, standard bodies, regulators, users and infrastructure operators owned different parts of evidence, implementation and consequence.
externalitiesAndCorrections: Lifecycle harms and authority changes are preserved where evidenced rather than inferred from local technical success.
secondOrderEffects: Computing shifted from custom electronic logic to a programmable component platform and then to ecosystems in which software, interfaces and third-party complements often mattered more than the CPU alone.
sourceNativeSummary: Computing shifted from custom electronic logic to a programmable component platform and then to ecosystems in which software, interfaces and third-party complements often mattered more than the CPU alone.
unresolvedHistoricalQuestions: Which complement most constrained diffusion at each lifecycle phase?
